result.summary: Menelaus tests the Greeks by proposing flight, and Diomedes rebukes him; Calchas urges that Achilles' son be fetched, and Ulysses and Diomedes sail to Scyros. Meanwhile Eurypylus, Hercules' grandson, arrives to aid Troy, is feasted, and dons a shield showing Hercules' labours. In battle he kills Nireus and Machaon and routs the Greeks to their ships until night stops the Trojans.

scenes.title: Menelaus tests the Greeks
scenes.summary: At dawn Menelaus proposes sailing home as a test. Tydeides angrily rejects it and calls for battle.
scenes.stakes: The Greeks risk losing their will to fight and the chance of victory after heavy losses.

scenes.title: Embassy sent to Scyros
scenes.summary: Calchas urges fetching Achilles' son. Ulysses and Tydeides agree, Menelaus promises Hermione, and they sail.
scenes.stakes: Without Achilles' son the Greeks may fail to take Troy in the tenth year.

scenes.title: Eurypylus welcomed in Troy
scenes.summary: Eurypylus arrives with his host and is welcomed by Paris and Helen. The Trojans feast while the Greeks watch.
scenes.stakes: Troy needs relief from slaughter; the Greeks fear a night attack on their ships.

scenes.title: The shield of Hercules
scenes.summary: Eurypylus arms; his shield depicts Hercules' labours. Paris urges him to defend Troy and he swears to win or die.
scenes.stakes: Eurypylus swears never to leave the fight except in victory or death.

scenes.title: Battle: Nireus and Machaon fall
scenes.summary: Armies clash. Eurypylus kills Nireus and Machaon; Podaleirius joins the fight, with a digression on the Nymphs' cave.
scenes.stakes: Greek champions die and their bodies risk capture.

scenes.title: Greeks routed to the ships
scenes.summary: Eurypylus drives the Greeks back. Many die on both sides until night stops the Trojans from burning the ships.
scenes.stakes: The Greek fleet faces burning and the army destruction.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable maxim on the power of desire.
Eurypylus' taunt over the fallen beautiful Nireus.
Teucer's maxim that glory requires toil.

analysis.text: The book shows war's cost and the Greeks' wavering morale, with a new Trojan champion renewing the struggle.
The long shield description follows the epic tradition of Homer's shield of Achilles, showing heroic ancestry through art.

legacy.text: The poem by Quintus of Smyrna continues the Iliad's story and was a major source for later accounts of Troy's fall.

fun_facts.text: Quintus Smyrnaeus's epic, also called Posthomerica, fills the gap between Homer's Iliad and Odyssey.

language_notes.text: Tithonus was a Trojan prince loved by Dawn (Eos), who took him as her husband; so Dawn rises from his bed.
A folkmote is an assembly of the people, here the army's general meeting.
Aias and Achilles, the greatest Greek warriors, have died earlier in the poem, which makes Menelaus's despair plausible.
"Chode" is an archaic past tense of "chide": he rebuked or scolded.
Tydeides is Diomedes, son of Tydeus; "Atreus' son" is Menelaus.
"Coronal of towers" means the crown-like ring of Troy's towers and walls.
A corslet is body armour protecting the chest; "whet" means to sharpen.
"Thestor's son" is Calchas, the seer, identified by his father's name; "in the midst" means in the middle of the assembly.
Tydeides is Diomedes, son of Tydeus. Achilles' son is Neoptolemus, raised on Scyros, whom prophecy says is needed to take Troy.
The Pierides are the Muses, named from Pieria, a region of Macedonia sacred to them.
"Suasion" means persuasion.
"I trow" means I believe; "sire-in-law" means father-in-law.
"Morning meat" means the morning meal; "meat" once meant food generally.
"Aweless" means fearless, not awed by anything; it is a recurring epithet in this translation.
The Caicus is a river in Mysia, in Asia Minor; Eurypylus's people live near its mouth.
Eurypylus is Priam's kinsman: his mother Astyoche was Priam's sister, and Telephus was his father, so he is Hector's cousin.
Telephus, the baby of Hercules and Auge, was exposed and, in legend, suckled by a hind (deer) before being rescued.
Assaracus was an early Trojan king, an ancestor of Priam; his tomb is a city landmark.
"Fane" means temple; "burg" means fortified town. Tritonis is Athena (Pallas), called by this cult title.
"Home-warder Zeus" is Zeus as protector of the household, with an altar near Paris's house.
"Hautboys" are oboe-like reed instruments; "Ceteian" refers to Eurypylus's Mysian followers, the Ceteians.
"Bright-throned Queen of Morn" is Dawn personified, a Homeric-style way of saying morning came.
Levin-flashes means lightning flashes; 'levin' is an archaic word for lightning.
Infant Hercules strangled the two serpents sent by Juno to kill him in his cradle.
Aweless means fearless, not affected by awe or dread.
Aleides (Alcides) is a name for Hercules, from his grandfather Alceus.
Hercules brought the Erymanthian Boar alive to King Eurystheus, who hid in a jar in terror; this was one of his twelve labours.
Hercules cleaned the filthy stables of Augeias in one labour by diverting the river Alpheius through them.
The Girdle of Hippolyta, Amazon queen, was taken as one of the labours at Eurystheus' command.
Cerberus, the three-headed hound of Hades, was dragged to the upper world as Hercules' last labour; Typho is Typhon, his monstrous father.
Hercules freed the Titan Prometheus, chained on Caucasus, by killing the eagle that ate his liver.
Goodlihead is an archaic word for goodliness, meaning comeliness or noble appearance.
'I trow' is archaic for 'I believe'.
'On the Gods' knees' is a Homeric idiom meaning the outcome rests with the gods.
Alexander is another name for Paris, the Trojan prince whose abduction of Helen caused the war.
A twibill is a double-bladed axe, a battle-axe with two cutting edges.
Zeus is named here, unlike the translation's usual Jove. Eurypylus's strength is a favour to Hercules, who was his grandfather's kin through his mother Astyoche, Priam's sister.
A leech is an old word for a physician; Eurypylus mocks Machaon's healing arts.
Weird means fate or destiny, what is decreed to happen.
Hale means drag or haul away by force; Ilium is another name for Troy.
The Parthenius is a river in Paphlagonia on the Black Sea (Euxine), the homeland of Cleitus.
Machaon, the Greek physician, had just been killed by Eurypylus; 'Aglaia's son' is Nireus, also slain. Both bodies are being fought over.
'Haply' means perhaps; 'Aias' is Ajax; 'Atreidae' are Agamemnon and Menelaus, sons of Atreus; 'Oileus' son' is the lesser Ajax.
'Battle-stay' means the mainstay or bulwark of the battle, here Eurypylus as the Trojans' chief support.
Caphaerus' rocks are where the Greek fleet was later wrecked on the voyage home; Oileus' son is fated to die there.
'Pales' are stakes or fences; 'thrall' is a slave or servant.
'Erewhile' means a short time before; 'waxed' means grew.
The poet says even iron lungs could not suffice to sing all the dead, echoing Homeric invocations of many voices.
'Had not night... uprisen' is a contrary-to-fact condition: the ships would have burned, but night intervened.

context_notes.text: Eurypylus, son of Telephus and grandson of Hercules, leads a Mysian force to aid Troy after the deaths of Trojan allies.
Ares is the god of war; to "glut Ares with blood" means to give him plentiful slaughter.
Calchas is the Greeks' chief seer, whose prophecies guide the army throughout the war.
Laertes' son is Ulysses, called Odysseus in the Greek; he is the army's cleverest speaker and negotiator.
Menelaus' wife Helen was taken by Paris, the cause of the war. Hermione is their daughter.
Eurypylus, son of Telephus and grandson of Hercules, comes as an ally to Troy after Hector's and Memnon's losses.
Helen, wife of Menelaus, was taken to Troy by Paris, which caused the war.
Argives is another name for the Greeks, used here for the besiegers watching from their camp.
Eurypylus, son of Telephus, leads the Mysians as a new ally of Troy after Hector's death.
Hercules saved Hesione, daughter of Laomedon king of Troy, from a sea-monster, making the shield's scene fitting for Troy's defender.
Paris, son of Priam, was the Trojan prince whose abduction of Helen caused the war.
Machaon is a renowned physician and son of Aesculapius, healer-god, serving the Greeks; he fights beside his brother Podaleirius.
Machaon's father is Aesculapius, god of healing; Eurypylus says even his divine father could not save him.
Danaans is another name for the Greeks, as are Argives.
Eurypylus, son of Telephus, is a Trojan ally who leads the Mysians and is the dominant fighter in this book.
Royal hunts penned wild beasts in enclosures so kings and people could watch them fight.
The Simois is one of the two rivers of the Trojan plain, near the Greek camp.

literary_notes.text: Dawn rises, climbs the heavens and scatters splendour while earth laughs, presenting morning as a living goddess and joyful world.
The narrator steps back to reflect on mortals as frail, dying creatures, adding a mournful, universal tone.
The narrator reveals the speech was only a test, so the reader knows Menelaus's despair is feigned while the army does not.
The narrator's general maxim about desire explains Menelaus's hidden thirst for vengeance.
Diomedes's gruesome threat of beheading and feeding kites shows fierce resolve and exaggerates his contempt for retreat.
Calchas' claim that victory lies at the Greeks' feet anticipates Troy's fall, which the poem's title announces.
Ulysses shows his tact and rhetorical skill by acknowledging the army's weariness before urging action.
Sound and motion words like "smote," "flashed" and "leapt" make the ship's departure vivid.
The rowers are compared to straining oxen dragging a wagon, stressing the labor and sweat of the voyage.
The Trojans crowding round Eurypylus are compared to tame geese around a feeder, suggesting their dependence and eager hope.
Eurypylus is likened to a lion among jackals, stressing his superior size and strength.
Fires, pipes, lyres and chatter fill the senses, painting the Trojan camp's confident revelry.
The Greeks watch the festive plain with unease, setting Trojan celebration against Greek wariness.
Eurypylus sleeps in Paris and Helen's own bower, a mark of honor that hints at how much Troy now stakes on him.
Armour compared to lightning flashes conveys the dazzling, fearsome look of the warrior.
The lion seems truly to gasp, stressing the shield's lifelike craftsmanship.
The detailed description of the shield's images makes the artwork seem to live and moves the narrative through pictures.
Likening Eurypylus to the War-god shows his terrifying stature and how the Trojans see him.
Paris urges Eurypylus to emulate Hercules, linking the shield's imagery to the hero's duty as Troy's saviour.
The oath 'victory or death' hints that Eurypylus will die in battle.
The Trojan host streaming after their leaders is compared to bees pouring from hives, suggesting orderly, noisy, eager movement.
The armies' joyful meeting is likened to calves meeting cows in spring pasture, a peaceful image that ironically contrasts with the coming slaughter.
Strife and Slaughter are made into walking figures, giving the battle a monstrous presence.
Nireus's fallen beauty is compared to an olive sapling uprooted by a flood, emphasizing youth and waste.
Eurypylus's blunt saying sums up his arrogance and the poem's theme that strength defeats beauty.
Machaon falling like a bull beneath a lion's jaws portrays Eurypylus as a predator.
Eurypylus's boast that not even a god pouring nectar could save Machaon exaggerates his power and shows his pride.
Machaon's dying prophecy hints that Eurypylus will soon meet his own death at Troy.
Eurypylus is called an avalanche of havoc, picturing his assault as an overwhelming natural force.
Rushing 'with eagle-swoop' compares Eurypylus to a diving bird of prey, stressing speed and menace.
The two kings surrounded by foes are compared to boars or lions penned in a hunt, still dangerous to anyone approaching.
Panic 'gripped the hearts' as if it were a hand, making fear an active force.
Eurypylus mocks the fleeing Greeks as scared sheep, belittling them.
The pursuing Trojans are like white-fanged hounds chasing deer through forest glens, making the Greeks helpless prey.
The narrator steps in personally, confessing the limits of his powers before so many deaths.
Night is pictured as trailing heavy mist, a divine rescuer that halts the burning of the ships.
